comparisons.peer_topic: Capital ratio table and transition periods
comparisons.peer_summary: The provided table presents capital ratios and related information in accordance with Basel 3 Standardized and Advanced approaches as measured at December 31, 2024 and 2023, with ratios calculated using a five-year transition period related to the adoption of the current expected credit losses accounting standard.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America disclose the regulatory capital rules allowing for a transition period related to CECL adoption. Goldman Sachs details the specific phasing in of the $1.11 billion capital reduction. Bank of America notes that its capital ratios are calculated using a regulatory capital rule that allows a five-year transition period related to the adoption of the CECL accounting standard.

sentences.text: • Beginning in January 2022, the firm started to phase in the estimated reduction to regulatory capital as a result of adopting the CECL model. The total amount of reduction to be phased in from January 1, 2022 through January 1, 2025 (at 25% per year) was $1.11 billion, of which $829 million had been phased in as of December 2024. The total amount to be phased in includes the impact of adopting CECL as of January 1, 2020, as well as 25% of the increase in the allowance for credit losses from January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2021. The impact of CECL transition reflects the remaining amount of reduction to be phased in as of both December 2024 and December 2023.

(1)As of December 31, 2024 and 2023, capital ratios are calculated using the regulatory capital rule that allows a five-year transition period related to the adoption of the current expected credit losses accounting standard on January 1, 2020.

peer_results.rationale: Citi's provided disclosures focus on the operational drivers of ACLL balances and the accounting impact of ASU 2022-02 adoption on retained earnings and assets, rather than the regulatory capital phase-out mechanics or CET1/Tier 2 capital transition provisions comparable to Goldman Sachs's disclosure.

comparisons.peer_summary: The $2.9 billion CECL capital benefit for CET1 is being phased out at 25% per year starting January 1, 2022, resulting in $720 million and $1.4 billion remaining benefits reflected in CET1 capital as of December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan disclose the specific phase-out schedule and remaining balance of the CECL regulatory capital transition benefit for CET1 capital. Goldman Sachs phased in an estimated $1.11 billion reduction over three years (25% per year), with $829 million phased in as of Dec 2024, leaving a remaining reduction to be phased in. JPMorgan similarly phased out a $2.9 billion CECL capital benefit at 25% per year starting Jan 1, 2022, reflecting a remaining benefit of $720 million in CET1 capital as of Dec 31, 2024.

Beginning January 1, 2022, the $2.9 billion CECL capital benefit, provided by the Federal Reserve in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, is being phased out at 25% per year over a three-year period.
As of December 31, 2024 and 2023, the Firm's CET1 capital reflected the remaining benefit of $720 million and $1.4 billion, respectively, associated with the CECL capital transition provisions.

comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm elected to defer the effect of CECL adoption on capital amounts and ratios over a five-year transition period starting January 1, 2020, with impacts phasing in at 25% annually from 2022, 75% from 2024, and fully phased in from 2025.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both disclose the implementation of the CECL transition phasing schedule, specifically noting the 25% annual phase-in rates starting in 2022. Goldman Sachs states its total reduction includes impacts from 2020 adoption and subsequent increases, phasing in at 25% per year. Morgan Stanley explicitly details a five-year transition period where impacts phased in at 25% per year from Jan 1, 2022, reaching 75% by Jan 1, 2024.

sentences.text: • Beginning in January 2022, the firm started to phase in the estimated reduction to regulatory capital as a result of adopting the CECL model. The total amount of reduction to be phased in from January 1, 2022 through January 1, 2025 (at 25% per year) was $1.11 billion, of which $829 million had been phased in as of December 2024. The total amount to be phased in includes the impact of adopting CECL as of January 1, 2020, as well as 25% of the increase in the allowance for credit losses from January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2021. The impact of CECL transition reflects the remaining amount of reduction to be phased in as of both December 2024 and December 2023.

Beginning on January 1, 2020, the Firm elected to defer the effect of the adoption of CECL on its risk-based and leverage-based capital amounts and ratios, as well as RWA, adjusted average assets and supplementary leverage exposure calculations, over a five-year transition period.
The deferral impacts began to phase in at 25% per year from January 1, 2022 and were phased-in at 75% from January 1, 2024.
